title: Operations With Decimals
bigQuestion: How do we add, subtract, multiply and divide decimals without losing track of the decimal point?

story.title: The Receipt That Did Not Add Up
story.kicker: A girl who can add decimals catches a cash register in a $3.98 mistake.
paragraphs: Rosa and her dad shop at a grocery store on Chicago's west side every Saturday. This week the list is short: milk, bread, apples and cereal. Rosa's job is to keep a running total in her head so they do not go over $15. She rounds each price and adds as they go. She gets about $14. Close, but under.

At the register the cashier scans the items and the screen says $18.49. Rosa frowns. She is sure she added right. Her dad pays, but Rosa keeps the receipt. In the car she adds the four prices carefully, lining up the dollars and the cents: $3.49, $2.79, $4.25 and $3.98.

The sum is $14.51. That is $3.98 less than the receipt. Rosa knows that number. It is the price of the cereal. She looks at the receipt again. There it is: cereal, scanned twice. The store owes them $3.98. They go back in, and the manager returns the money with an apology.

Rosa caught the mistake because she could add decimals and check with an estimate. Money is decimals: dollars to the left of the point, cents to the right. So are meters, liters and kilograms. Every day, people add, subtract, multiply and divide these numbers, and machines sometimes get it wrong.

This chapter teaches those operations. You will line up decimal points and regroup across the point. You will move the point when you multiply or divide by ten. You will count decimal places when you multiply. Most of all, you will learn to check your work. Then a bad receipt will never fool you.
story.think: Rosa's estimate was about $14, and the receipt said $18.49. How did the estimate alone tell her something was wrong?

lessons.title: Lining Up the Point
lessons.mainIdea: To add decimals, line up the decimal points so each place sits under the same place, then add like whole numbers.
reading: Add 3.49 + 2.75. Write one under the other with the decimal points in a straight line. Hundredths under hundredths, tenths under tenths, ones under ones. Add the hundredths: 9 + 5 = 14. Write 4 and *regroup* 1 to the tenths. Tenths: 4 + 7 + 1 = 12. Write 2, regroup 1. Ones: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Bring the point straight down. The *sum* is 6.24.

Now add 5.8 + 2.36. The numbers have different lengths. Give 5.8 a zero: 5.80. Now line up 5.80 + 2.36. Hundredths: 0 + 6 = 6. Tenths: 8 + 3 = 11, write 1, regroup 1. Ones: 5 + 2 + 1 = 8. Answer: 8.16. The zero did not change 5.8, but it kept the places lined up.

The big mistake is lining up the right ends instead of the points. Someone adds 5.8 + 2.36 that way and gets 2.94, treating 5.8 as 0.58. Always line up the points first. Then check with an *estimate*: 5.8 is about 6, and 2.36 is about 2, so the sum should be near 8. And 8.16 is near 8. Good.

words.d: the answer to an addition problem
to carry 10 of one place into 1 of the next bigger place, like 14 hundredths into 1 tenth and 4 hundredths
a quick, rough answer made with rounded numbers, used to check the exact answer

look.title: Two Cans of Paint
look.text: A can of blue paint weighs 4.35 kilograms. A can of white paint weighs 3.9 kilograms. A painter lifts both cans into a truck at once. To find the total, she writes 4.35 over 3.90 with the points lined up.
look.prompt: What is the total mass? Estimate first, then add. How do you know the answer is not 4.74?

check.why: Write 2.60 + 1.35. Hundredths 0 + 5 = 5, tenths 6 + 3 = 9, ones 2 + 1 = 3. Sum: 3.95.
Write 7.48 + 0.90. Tenths 4 + 9 = 13, write 3, regroup 1. Ones 7 + 0 + 1 = 8. Sum: 8.38.

check.q: Why do you line up the decimal points when adding?
choices: so you can add left to right
so the answer has fewer digits
so tenths add to tenths and hundredths add to hundredths
check.why: Only equal places can be added together. Lining up the points puts each place under the same place.

lessons.title: Subtracting With Regrouping
lessons.mainIdea: Subtract decimals the way you add them: line up the points, fill empty places with zeros, and regroup when a digit is too small.
reading: Subtract 6.25 − 2.8. Line up the points and add a zero: 6.25 − 2.80. Hundredths: 5 − 0 = 5. Tenths: 2 − 8 will not work. Regroup: take 1 from the 6 ones, making it 5, and give 10 tenths to the 2, making 12. Now 12 − 8 = 4. Ones: 5 − 2 = 3. The *difference* is 3.45. Check by adding back: 3.45 + 2.8 = 6.25. Yes.

Subtract 5 − 1.37. The 5 has no decimal places, so write it as 5.00. Hundredths: 0 − 7 needs regrouping, but the tenths are 0 too. Regroup twice: 5.00 becomes 4 ones, 9 tenths, 10 hundredths. Now 10 − 7 = 3, then 9 − 3 = 6, then 4 − 1 = 3. Answer: 3.63. Add back to check: 3.63 + 1.37 = 5.00.

Making *change* is subtraction. You pay $10 for a $7.45 item. Change is 10.00 − 7.45 = 2.55. A common mistake is subtracting the smaller digit from the bigger one no matter which is on top, giving 3.45. Always regroup instead. Another mistake is forgetting to write 5 as 5.00. Empty places are zeros.

words.d: the answer to a subtraction problem
the money you get back when you pay more than the price

look.title: The Runner's Best Time
look.text: Keisha ran the 400 meters in 72.4 seconds in April. In May she ran it in 69.85 seconds. Her coach asks how much time she cut. Keisha writes 72.40 above 69.85 with the points lined up and starts regrouping.
look.prompt: How many seconds faster was May? Show the two regroupings you need, and check by adding back.

check.why: Write 9.30 − 4.85. Regroup twice: 10 − 5 = 5, 12 − 8 = 4, 8 − 4 = 4. Difference: 4.45.
Write 8.00 − 3.29. Regroup to 7 ones, 9 tenths, 10 hundredths: 10 − 9 = 1, 9 − 2 = 7, 7 − 3 = 4. Answer: 4.71.

check.q: You pay with a $20 bill for a $13.65 item. What is your change?

lessons.title: Estimating Sums and Differences
lessons.mainIdea: Round each decimal to a friendly number first; the estimate tells you whether your exact answer makes sense.
reading: A shopper picks up items priced $4.89, $2.15 and $6.95. Is $20 enough? Round each to a *friendly number*, the nearest dollar: 5 + 2 + 7 = 14. That is under 20, so yes. The *exact answer* is 4.89 + 2.15 + 6.95 = 13.99, close to the estimate of 14. Estimating is fast and catches big errors.

Estimate 15.62 − 8.9. Round to whole numbers: 16 − 9 = 7. Exact: 15.62 − 8.90 = 6.72. That is close to 7, so the exact answer is likely right. If your exact answer were 14.73, the estimate would warn you. Something went wrong, probably lining up the right ends instead of the points.

Sometimes round to tenths for a closer estimate. 3.48 + 2.71 rounds to 3.5 + 2.7 = 6.2. Exact: 6.19. A common mistake is rounding after adding, which is not estimating at all. Round first, then add. Another mistake is always rounding down. Use the rounding rule: 4.89 goes to 5, not 4.

words.d: a rounded number that is easy to add or subtract in your head, like 5 instead of 4.89
the true answer found by computing with the real numbers, not rounded ones

look.title: Four Items on a Receipt
look.prompt: Estimate the total by rounding each price to the nearest dollar. Then find the exact total. How far apart are they?

check.why: 7.92 rounds to 8 and 3.18 rounds to 3. So 8 + 3 = 11. The exact sum, 11.10, is close.

check.q: Estimate 24.6 − 9.85 by rounding to whole numbers.
check.why: 24.6 rounds to 25 and 9.85 rounds to 10. So 25 − 10 = 15.

check.q: A student adds 6.3 + 2.48 and gets 3.11. What does an estimate show?
choices: The answer is right, since 6 + 2 is about 3
The answer is wrong, since 6 + 2 is about 8
check.why: 6 + 2 = 8, so the sum must be near 8. The student lined up the right ends. The true sum is 8.78.

lessons.title: Multiplying by 10, 100 and 1,000
lessons.mainIdea: Multiplying by 10 makes every digit worth 10 times more, so the decimal point shifts one place to the right; by 100, two places; by 1,000, three.
reading: One pencil costs $0.35. Ten pencils cost 0.35 × 10. Think in cents: 35 cents times 10 is 350 cents, or $3.50. Look at the digits: 0.35 became 3.50. The point moved one place to the right. That always happens when you multiply by 10, because every digit is worth 10 times more. Tenths become ones. Hundredths become tenths.

Multiply by 100 and the point moves two places. So 0.35 × 100 = 35. Multiply by 1,000 and it moves three: 0.35 × 1,000 = 350. When you run out of digits, add zeros. Try 2.7 × 1,000. Move three places. 2.7 has only one digit after the point, so write 2.700 first, then move: 2,700. Each *power of ten* moves the point one more place.

A common mistake is adding a zero to the end, like 2.7 × 10 = 2.70. That is the same number, not ten times more. Move the point instead: 27. Check with sense: ten things at $2.70 each should cost more than $2.70. Another check: 2.7 × 10 is about 3 × 10 = 30, and the *product* 27 is near 30.

words.d: 10, 100, 1,000 and so on; each one is ten times the one before
the answer to a multiplication problem

look.title: Water Bottles at $0.85 Each
look.prompt: How does the decimal point move as you go down the table? What would 10,000 bottles cost?

check.why: Multiplying by 10 moves the point one place right: 4.06 becomes 40.6.
Move the point two places right. 0.9 becomes 0.90, then 90.
Move the point three places right. 1.25 becomes 1.250, then 1,250.

lessons.title: Multiplying a Decimal by a Whole Number
lessons.mainIdea: Multiply as if there were no decimal point, then place the point so the product has as many decimal places as the decimal factor.
reading: Three friends each run 2.4 kilometers. Total: 2.4 × 3. One way: add 2.4 + 2.4 + 2.4 = 7.2. Another way: ignore the point, 24 × 3 = 72. The *factor* 2.4 has one of the *decimal places*, so the product needs one too: 7.2. Both ways agree. Picture it: 2 whole kilometers three times is 6, plus 4 tenths three times is 12 tenths, or 1.2. Total 7.2.

Try 1.35 × 4. Ignore the point: 135 × 4 = 540. Count decimal places in 1.35: two. Put the point two places from the right: 5.40, which is 5.4. Check with an estimate: 1.35 is a bit more than 1, so 4 of them is a bit more than 4. Yes, 5.4 fits.

A common mistake is dropping the point and answering 540. Estimating catches it: 1.35 × 4 cannot be 540. Another mistake is counting the whole number's digits. The whole number has no decimal places. Only the decimal factor counts. With money, think in cents: $1.35 is 135 cents, times 4 is 540 cents, which is $5.40.

words.d: a number being multiplied; in 2.4 × 3, both 2.4 and 3 are factors
the number of digits to the right of the decimal point; 1.35 has two

look.title: Train Fares for the Field Trip
look.text: A class of 24 students rides the train to a museum. Each student fare is $1.25. The teacher wants the total before she buys the tickets. She writes 125 × 24 first, then decides where the decimal point goes.
look.prompt: What is the total? How many decimal places does the product need, and why?

check.why: 32 × 6 = 192. One decimal place in 3.2, so the product is 19.2. Check: 3 × 6 = 18, close.
75 × 8 = 600. Two decimal places: 6.00, which is 6. Check: 0.75 is three quarters, and 8 quarters make 2 dollars, so 6.

check.q: Each notebook costs $2.45. What do 5 notebooks cost?
check.why: 245 × 5 = 1,225. Two decimal places: $12.25. Check: 5 × 2.50 = 12.50, close.

lessons.title: Multiplying Two Decimals
lessons.mainIdea: When both factors are decimals, count the decimal places in both, add the counts, and give the product that many places.
reading: A tile is 0.5 meters wide and 0.3 meters tall. Its *area* is 0.5 × 0.3. Picture a hundredths grid: 5 columns wide and 3 rows tall covers 15 small squares. That is 15 hundredths, 0.15. Now check with the rule. Ignore the points: 5 × 3 = 15. Count decimal places: 0.5 has one, 0.3 has one, total two. So 0.15.

Try 1.2 × 0.4. Ignore the points: 12 × 4 = 48. Decimal places: 1.2 has one, 0.4 has one, total two. Product: 0.48. Estimate to check: 1.2 × 0.4 is a bit more than 1 × 0.4 = 0.4. Yes. Try 2.5 × 1.5: 25 × 15 = 375, two places, 3.75. That is a bit more than 2.5 × 1 = 2.5. Yes.

Multiplying by a decimal less than 1 makes a number smaller. So 0.5 × 0.3 = 0.15 is less than both factors. Students who expect a bigger answer sometimes write 1.5. Count the places. A common mistake is placing the point by lining it up, as in addition. Multiplication does not line up points. It counts them.

words.d: the amount of flat space a shape covers, found for a rectangle by length × width
the number of digits to the right of the decimal point; 0.48 has two

look.title: The Quilt Rectangle
look.text: A quilt piece is 1.5 meters long and 0.8 meters wide. To find its area, multiply 15 × 8 first. Then count the decimal places in the two lengths. One student writes 12.0 square meters. Another writes 1.20 square meters.
look.prompt: Which student is right? Explain using the count of decimal places and an estimate.

check.why: 6 × 7 = 42. One place plus one place is two places: 0.42.
25 × 4 = 100. Two decimal places: 1.00, which is 1. Check: 0.4 of 2.5 is less than 2.5.
9 × 9 = 81, two decimal places, 0.81. Multiplying by a number less than 1 makes the result smaller.

lessons.title: Dividing by 10, 100 and 1,000
lessons.mainIdea: Dividing by 10 makes every digit worth 10 times less, so the decimal point shifts one place to the left; by 100, two; by 1,000, three.
reading: Ten friends split a $24.50 bill evenly. Each pays 24.50 ÷ 10. To *divide* by 10, make every digit 10 times smaller. The point moves one place left: 2.45. Each pays $2.45. Check: 2.45 × 10 = 24.50. Dividing by 10 undoes multiplying by 10. The answer, 2.45, is called the *quotient*.

Divide by 100 and the point moves two places left: 24.5 ÷ 100 = 0.245. Divide by 1,000 and it moves three: 24.5 ÷ 1,000 = 0.0245. Add zeros when you need them. Try 7 ÷ 100: write 7 as 7.0, move two places, 0.07. Seven cents is 7 ÷ 100 of a dollar.

This is how metric units convert. 350 centimeters ÷ 100 = 3.5 meters. 1,750 meters ÷ 1,000 = 1.75 kilometers. A common mistake is moving the point the wrong way. Ask: should the answer be bigger or smaller? Dividing by 10 makes it smaller, so the point goes left. So 6.4 ÷ 10 is 0.64, not 64.

words.d: to split a number into equal groups, or to find how many times one number fits in another
the answer to a division problem

look.title: Sharing $360 Evenly
look.prompt: Where does the decimal point move each time the group gets 10 times bigger? What would each of 10,000 people get?

check.why: Dividing by 10 moves the point one place left: 53.8 becomes 5.38.
Write 6 as 6.0 and move the point two places left: 0.06.
Divide by 1,000: move the point three places left. 4,250 becomes 4.25 km.

lessons.title: Dividing a Decimal by a Whole Number
lessons.mainIdea: Divide as with whole numbers, and put the decimal point in the quotient straight above the point in the number being divided.
reading: Four friends share 9.6 pounds of apples. Each gets 9.6 ÷ 4. The 9.6 is the *dividend*. Place the point in the answer right above the point in 9.6. Divide the ones: 9 ÷ 4 is 2, with a *remainder* of 1. That 1 one is 10 tenths. Add the 6 tenths: 16 tenths. Then 16 ÷ 4 = 4. Answer: 2.4 pounds each. Check: 2.4 × 4 = 9.6.

Sometimes you must add a zero. Divide 7.5 ÷ 6. Ones: 7 ÷ 6 = 1, remainder 1. Tenths: 15 ÷ 6 = 2, remainder 3. Write 7.5 as 7.50 and keep going. Hundredths: 30 ÷ 6 = 5. Answer: 1.25. Check: 1.25 × 6 = 7.50. Adding zeros on the right never changes the number, so you may keep dividing.

A common mistake is dropping the point and writing 24 instead of 2.4. Estimate: 9.6 ÷ 4 is about 10 ÷ 4, between 2 and 3. So 24 cannot be right. Another mistake is forgetting the leftover ones. In 9 ÷ 4 the remainder 1 must join the tenths. Every leftover moves to the next smaller place.

words.d: the number being divided; in 9.6 ÷ 4, the dividend is 9.6
what is left over after dividing one place, which moves to the next smaller place

look.title: Cutting the Ribbon
look.text: A spool holds 8.4 meters of ribbon. A teacher cuts it into 7 equal pieces for bows. She sets up 8.4 ÷ 7 and puts the decimal point in the answer first, right above the point in 8.4. Then she divides the ones, carries the leftover to the tenths, and divides again.
look.prompt: How long is each piece? Check your answer by multiplying it by 7.

check.why: 6 ÷ 8 is 0 with 6 left over. That is 60 tenths, plus 4 is 64 tenths. 64 ÷ 8 = 8 tenths: 0.8. Check: 0.8 × 8 = 6.4.

check.q: Three friends split a $13.50 bill evenly. How much does each pay?
check.why: 13 ÷ 3 = 4, remainder 1. Then 15 tenths ÷ 3 = 5 tenths. So $4.50 each. Check: 4.50 × 3 = 13.50.
36 tenths ÷ 5 = 7 tenths, remainder 1 tenth = 10 hundredths, and 10 ÷ 5 = 2. So 0.72. Check: 0.72 × 5 = 3.60.

lessons.title: Money Word Problems
lessons.mainIdea: Read the story, decide which operation it asks for, line up the dollars and cents, and check the answer with an estimate.
reading: Dev has $15.00. He buys a book for $8.75 and a pen for $1.60. How much is left? First the *total* spent: 8.75 + 1.60 = 10.35. Then the money left: 15.00 − 10.35 = 4.65. Two steps, two operations. Estimate: 9 + 2 = 11, and 15 − 11 = 4. The exact $4.65 is close to 4, so it fits.

A pack of 6 juice boxes costs $4.50. What does one cost? Divide: 4.50 ÷ 6. Think in cents: 450 ÷ 6 = 75. So $0.75 each, or 75 cents *per* box. What do 4 packs cost? Multiply: 4.50 × 4 = 18.00. The words tell the *operation*. 'Each' with a total means divide. 'Each' with a count means multiply.

A common mistake is doing only one step. Dev's problem asks what is left, not what he spent. Answering $10.35 stops too early. Another mistake is mixing units, adding $1.60 to 875 cents. Keep everything in dollars or everything in cents. Write the final answer with a dollar sign and two decimal places.

words.d: one of the four ways to combine numbers: add, subtract, multiply or divide
the whole amount when parts are put together
for each one, as in 75 cents per box

look.title: The Corrected Receipt
look.text: A receipt lists milk $3.49, bread $2.79, apples $4.25 and cereal $3.98, but the total says $18.49. The shopper adds the four prices herself and gets $14.51. She looks again and sees the cereal was scanned twice.
look.prompt: Show that $14.51 plus one extra cereal makes the receipt total. How much should the store give back?

check.q: Mia has $20. She spends $6.45 and $3.80. How much is left?
Five tickets cost $31.25 in all. What does one ticket cost?
Which operation finds the cost of 7 items at $2.30 each?
check.why: 'Each' with a count of items means multiply. 2.30 × 7 = 16.10.

lessons.title: Measurement Word Problems
lessons.mainIdea: Measurement problems with decimals work like money problems: match the units, line up the places, then add, subtract, multiply or divide.
reading: A board is 2.4 meters long. A carpenter cuts off 0.85 meters. How much is left? Subtract: 2.40 − 0.85 = 1.55 meters. Then she cuts the rest into 5 equal shelves. Divide: 1.55 ÷ 5. In hundredths, 155 ÷ 5 = 31, so 0.31 meters each. Check: 0.31 × 5 = 1.55.

A recipe needs 0.75 *liters* of milk. You make 3 batches. Multiply: 0.75 × 3 = 2.25 liters. Your carton holds 2 liters. Is that enough? 2.25 > 2, so no. You are short by 2.25 − 2.00 = 0.25 liters. Compare the *units* first: both are liters, so the numbers can be compared directly.

When units differ, *convert* first. A path is 1.2 km and a second path is 850 m. Total? Change 850 m to 0.85 km. Then 1.2 + 0.85 = 2.05 km. A common mistake is adding 1.2 + 850 to get 851.2. The units did not match. Another mistake is writing 850 m as 8.5 km. Divide by 1,000: 0.85 km.

words.d: the basic metric unit for liquids; a large soda bottle holds about 2 liters
the thing being counted or measured, like meters, liters or dollars
to change a measurement from one unit to another, like 850 m to 0.85 km

look.title: Rain in One Week
look.prompt: Find the total rain for the week. Which day had the most? How much more fell Tuesday than Thursday?

check.q: A rope is 5.5 m long. You cut off 1.75 m. How much is left?
A bottle holds 0.5 liters. How many liters do 12 bottles hold?
check.why: 5 × 12 = 60. One decimal place: 6.0 liters. Check: 12 half-liters make 6 liters.

check.q: A trail is 2.3 km and another is 700 m. What is the total in kilometers?
check.why: Convert 700 m to 0.7 km. Then 2.3 + 0.7 = 3.0 km.

review.why: Write 4.70 + 3.85. Tenths 7 + 8 = 15, write 5, regroup 1. Ones 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. Sum: 8.55.
Move the point two places right: 0.8 becomes 0.80, then 80.
27 × 3 = 81. One place plus one place is two places: 0.81.
Move the point three places left. 45.2 becomes 0.0452.

review.q: Six friends split $27.00 evenly. How much does each pay?
review.why: 27 ÷ 6 = 4, remainder 3. Then 30 tenths ÷ 6 = 5 tenths. So $4.50. Check: 4.50 × 6 = 27.00.
5.92 rounds to 6 and 3.1 rounds to 3, so the sum should be near 9. The exact sum is 9.02.
